rv.tip.workers: How many engines search at once. A game's positions are independent, so two engines finish the pass in about half the time -- the same trick chess.com's review uses. The Threads below are SPLIT between them, so more engines means less depth each: two is the sweet spot on most machines, one is the old behaviour.
panel.tip.re_detect_the_game_rescan: Re-detect the game: rescan the page and restart the analysis
panel.tip.set_up_a_position_paste: Set up a position: paste a FEN to analyse it instead of the board on the page. While a position is set the panel stops following the page; click again (or Re-detect) to go back to the live game.
panel.tip.read_the_position_off_the: Read the position off the screen: captures this tab, finds the board and loads it into the panel. Works on any site (a video, a diagram, an image). If no board is found you can drag a box around it.
panel.tip.self_test_check_scraping_the: Self-test: check scraping, the engine, and the native host
panel.tip.copy_the_game_so_far: Copy the game so far as PGN
panel.tip.while_the_opponent_thinks_cert: While the opponent thinks, certify a reply to their predicted move -- stable across the Premove Confidence window, or, on a Maia engine, produced by a second inference of the same net on the predicted position. If they play exactly that move, answer instantly; anything else searches normally. If the reply could never be legal after any other opponent move (forced moves, recaptures), it's queued as a real premove immediately -- an illegal premove gets auto-cancelled. Never fires in a wrong position. Needs Autoplay.
panel.tip.show_how_humans_actually_playe: Show how humans actually played this opening (lichess database): the opening name plus the most-played replies with their win/draw/loss split. Read-out only -- it never changes which move you play. Standard chess only; stops once the game leaves book.
panel.tip.play_the_opening_from_the: Play the opening from the database instead of the engine's pick: a WEIGHTED-RANDOM choice among the popular replies, so you don't repeat the same line every game. A move must be played in at least 20 games AND rate within 40cp of the engine's best, so it varies without playing worse. Falls back to the engine move if the lookup hasn't arrived. Priority - Move: Book > Humanize > engine best. Needs Autoplay.
panel.tip.draws_the_best_move_as: Draws the best move as an arrow on the game board so you can play it yourself. Overrides Autoplay while on.
panel.tip.show_a_vertical_evaluation_bar: Show a vertical evaluation bar to the left of the game board, with the score shown inside it (chess.com-style).
panel.tip.a_graph_under_the_board: A graph under the board showing the whole game so far: white's advantage above the midline, black's below, with the opening/middlegame/endgame boundaries marked. Needs Eval Bar.
panel.tip.with_7_or_fewer_pieces: With 7 or fewer pieces left the position is solved: ask a Syzygy tablebase for the perfect move instead of trusting the search. Outranks the engine and the opening book. Answers from your local files when configured, lichess's online tablebase otherwise. Off by default -- the online lookup sends the position to a third party. Never delays a move.
panel.tip.play_like_a_human_instant: Play like a human: instant recaptures and forced moves, quick obvious moves, long thinks in critical positions -- and occasionally a second-best move, a mistake, or (rarely) a blunder. Priority - Time: Mirror > Clock > Humanize > Search Time (first one enabled sets the duration; recaptures & forced moves always instant). Move: Humanize > engine best.
panel.tip.read_the_game_clock_off: Read the game clock off the page and budget every move to it: roughly time/30 plus 60% of the increment, shrinking the engine search too, near-instant when short on time. Priority - Time: Mirror > Clock > Humanize > Search Time (first one enabled sets the duration; recaptures & forced moves always instant). Move: Humanize > engine best.
panel.tip.pace_to_the_opponent_instead: Pace to the opponent instead: spend what they spent on their last move, minus 10%, staying just ahead on the clock (30% extra haste when behind). Uses the Clock Mode budget for the first move / when their spend is unknown. Recaptures and forced moves stay instant. Priority - Time: Mirror > Clock > Humanize > Search Time (first one enabled sets the duration; recaptures & forced moves always instant). Move: Humanize > engine best.
panel.tip.the_engine_keeps_thinking_unti: The engine keeps thinking until YOU press the play-move hotkey (Spacebar by default), then it plays the best move it has found. Your own timing - overrides Clock/Mirror/Humanize timing and never fires on its own. Rebind the key in Settings → Hotkeys.
panel.tip.cap_the_engine_s_strength: Cap the engine's strength to a target Elo (UCI_LimitStrength + UCI_Elo). The slider stops follow the selected engine's own range (SF dev/18: 1320-3190, SF 11: 1350-2850, Fairy: 500-2850). Both ends mean full strength (no cap): Off on the far left, or past the engine's own max on the far right.
panel.tip.maia_3_target_rating_one: Maia-3 target rating. One transformer model conditioned on the Elo you set, so it plays like a human of that strength - anywhere from 600 to 2600, in fine steps. Changing it applies instantly (no reload).
panel.tip.which_maia_network_to_use: Which Maia network to use. Each is trained on human games at that rating, so it plays like a human of that strength - human-like mistakes, not a strong engine told to play badly. Changing this loads a different net.
panel.not_detected_hint:
If your chess game is not detected
try reloading the page
set.note.the_panel_button_row_bottom: The panel button row (bottom left) also has a set-up-position button — the grid icon beside Self-test. It opens a box to paste a FEN: press Enter and that position is analysed instead of the board on the page. While one is set the panel stops following the page so it cannot be overwritten; click the button again (or Re-detect) to return to the live game. An invalid or illegal FEN is refused with a reason.
set.note.the_floating_panel_is_embedded: ⚠️ The floating panel is embedded in the web page, which makes the extension easier for a chess site to detect. The toolbar popup runs entirely in the browser and leaves no page footprint - the safer choice for pure analysis. Note: the popup closes when you click the board, so Autoplay and Premove work only with the Floating panel.
set.note.download_lichess_db_puzzle_csv: Download lichess_db_puzzle.csv.zst from database.lichess.org, decompress it (unzstd lichess_db_puzzle.csv.zst), then pick the .csv here. It is about six million positions, so the import takes roughly half an hour - leave this page open. It only has to be done once, and if it is interrupted nothing is lost: run it again and it picks up what is missing.
set.note.keyboard_shortcuts_that_work_wh: Keyboard shortcuts that work while you're on the game page (they only fire when the floating panel is open). Click a key to rebind it - the next key you press (with any Ctrl/Alt/Shift/Meta) becomes the binding; press Esc to cancel, or Backspace/Delete to clear it. Defaults are single letters; the play-move key is Spacebar. If one clashes with a shortcut the site itself uses, rebind it with any Ctrl/Alt/Shift/Meta combination.
set.tip.mephisto_communicates_with_a_che: Which engine evaluates positions. WASM engines run inside this browser; the local ones need their native host installed; Remote Engine needs remote-engine.py (in "src/scripts") running. The two Cloud entries are a real Stockfish on somebody else's server: they need nothing installed, which is the point on a machine that cannot run a strong engine, but THE POSITION LEAVES YOUR MACHINE on every move. A local engine is both faster and private, so cloud is a fallback, not an upgrade. Cloud searches by depth (12 by default, capped at 18 on chess-api.com and 15 on stockfish.online) and returns one line.
set.tip.cap_the_engine_s_playing: Cap the engine's playing strength to a target Elo (sent as UCI_LimitStrength + UCI_Elo). The valid range follows the engine (SF dev/18: 1320-3190, SF 11: 1350-2850, Fairy: 500-2850), and out-of-range values are ignored (not clamped). 0 = full strength (no cap).
set.tip.position_changes_are_detected_in: Position changes are detected instantly (event-driven). This is only a slow safety-net poll that heals a missed update; 1000ms is fine.
set.tip.how_the_mephisto_panel_is: How the Mephisto panel is shown. Floating = the draggable window over the board; it lives in the page, so a chess site can detect it more easily. Toolbar popup = the classic bubble in the browser toolbar; it leaves NO trace in the page (the safer choice).
set.tip.mephisto_plays_as_the_brain: Mephisto plays as the "Brain", choosing which piece type to move, and you play as the "Hand", selecting the specific legal move for that piece.
set.tip.while_the_opponent_thinks_certif: While the opponent thinks, certify a reply to their predicted move. If they play exactly that move, answer instantly; anything else searches normally. Never fires in a wrong position. On chess.com, when the line is forced two moves deep -- their move is their only legal one, and after your reply they are forced again -- BOTH of your replies are queued at once (double premove). Needs Autoplay.
set.tip.use_the_opponent_s_thinking: Use the opponent's thinking time. ON: keep searching at full threads while it's the opponent's turn, so a deeper reply is ready the moment they move over their top 5 candidate replies -- they won't play the engine's #1 -- narrowing to 1-2 on a forced move or recapture (pairs with Premove for instant answers). OFF (default): the opponent's turn is still analysed for premove/threat/help, but capped to 2 threads so idle time isn't a full-core burn (never more than the Threads slider).
set.tip.with_7_or_fewer_pieces: With 7 or fewer pieces left the position is SOLVED, and Mephisto asks a Syzygy tablebase for the perfect move instead of trusting the search. It outranks the engine and the opening book. With a local tablebase configured below, the answer comes off YOUR files and nothing leaves the machine; otherwise it asks lichess's online tablebase. OFF by default: the online lookup sends the position to a third party, and the tables themselves are hundreds of gigabytes, so they can't be bundled. The lookup never delays a move -- if the answer is late, the engine's move is played.
set.tip.name_the_tactic_behind_the: Name the tactic behind the engine's move -- a fork, a promotion, a capture that wins material, mate -- on its own line under the evaluation. Deliberately conservative: pins, skewers and discovered attacks can't be established reliably from the position alone, so it says nothing rather than guessing. A confidently wrong explanation teaches the wrong thing.
set.tip.blurs_your_opponent_s_username: Blurs your opponent's username and avatar on the page, so a screenshot or a screen share does not expose a real person. Purely cosmetic and local -- the site sees nothing different. This is the one option that adds a style element to the page, so it is off unless you turn it on.
set.tip.show_how_humans_actually_played: Show how humans actually played this opening (lichess database): the opening name plus the most-played replies and their win/draw/loss split, in a block under the analysis lines. Read-out only -- it never changes which move you play. Standard chess only, and it stops once the game leaves book.
set.tip.play_the_opening_from_the: Play the opening from the database instead of the engine's pick: a WEIGHTED-RANDOM choice among the popular replies, so you don't repeat the same line every game -- an engine that always plays the same first move is itself a tell. A candidate must appear in at least 20 games AND rate within 40cp of the engine's own best, so the variety never costs you a worse move. If the lookup hasn't arrived by the time the move is due, the engine move is played instead -- it never delays a move. Priority -- Move: Book > Humanize > engine best. Needs Autoplay.
set.tip.own_book: Load your own Polyglot .bin and Play Book Moves plays from IT instead of the online database: same weighted-random pick, same never-delays-a-move rule, and the engine takes over at the first position the book does not know. One book at a time -- loading another replaces it. Stored on this machine only, works offline, and a file that is not a Polyglot book is refused when you load it, not discovered mid-game.
set.tip.tb_local: Choose the folder holding your Syzygy files (.rtbw/.rtbz) and the Endgame Tablebase answers from YOUR files instead of the network -- decoded right in the browser, nothing installed, nothing copied, nothing about the position leaves this computer, works offline. Only the folder's location is remembered; the browser may ask once per session to re-allow reading it. A position your set does not cover, or one with castling rights, falls back to the online lookup automatically. Check lists what the folder holds.
set.tip.tb_path: Alternative to the folder picker above: a filesystem path probed by the native engine host (needs native-host/install.sh). Only consulted when no picked folder answers. Leave empty unless you use the native hosts.
set.tip.which_games_the_opening_data: Which games the opening data comes from. Masters is the cleanest opening play. The Lichess sets are ordinary online games, so they look more like a normal opponent -- pick the club band to match a typical rating pool.
set.tip.when_off_default_moves_only: When OFF (default), moves only fire while this tab is focused and visible -- a human doesn't play while tabbed away, so this avoids a 'moved in the background' anomaly. A move that comes due while you're away is re-issued when you return. Turn ON to keep autoplay/premove running when the tab is hidden or unfocused. Note that keeping a hidden tab running requires marking it as playing audio (Chrome throttles silent background tabs), so the tab shows a speaker icon while this is on.
set.tip.instead_of_autoplaying_all_analy: Instead of autoplaying, all analysis arrows are drawn directly on the site's board while the engine keeps evaluating -- play the move yourself when ready. Overrides Autoplay while on.
set.tip.play_like_a_human_instant: Play like a human: instant recaptures and forced moves, quick obvious moves, long thinks in critical positions -- and occasionally a second-best move, a mistake, or (rarely) a blunder. Priority -- Time: Mirror > Clock > Humanize > Search Time (first one enabled sets the duration; recaptures & forced moves always instant). Move: Humanize > engine best.
set.tip.read_the_game_clock_off: Read the game clock off the page and budget thinking + search to it: roughly time/30 plus 60% of the increment per move, near-instant when short on time. Priority -- Time: Mirror > Clock > Humanize > Search Time (first one enabled sets the duration; recaptures & forced moves always instant). Move: Humanize > engine best.
set.tip.pace_to_the_opponent_instead: Pace to the opponent instead: spend what they spent on their last move, minus 10%, staying just ahead on the clock (30% extra haste when behind). Falls back to the Clock Mode budget when their spend is unknown. Recaptures and forced moves stay instant. Priority -- Time: Mirror > Clock > Humanize > Search Time (first one enabled sets the duration; recaptures & forced moves always instant). Move: Humanize > engine best.
set.tip.the_engine_keeps_thinking_until: The engine keeps thinking until YOU press the play-move hotkey (Spacebar by default -- rebind it under Hotkeys below), then it plays the best move it has found. Your own timing: overrides the Clock/Mirror/Humanize timing and never fires on its own.
set.tip.flash_a_small_toast_over: Flash a small toast over the board when your OPPONENT slips. When Move Classification has graded the move, the toast names the verdict -- Blunder, Miss, Mistake or Inaccuracy, including a Miss (a win let go) the plain win-drop rule cannot see; otherwise it falls back to the win% drop bands (30/20/10%). Only fires when both positions were searched deep enough to trust, so it won't invent blunders from shallow evals.
set.tip.mephisto_optimizes_for_solving_c: Mephisto optimizes for solving chess puzzles as quickly as possible, at the expense of accuracy. This should be enabled when autoplaying puzzle minigames, like Chess.com's Puzzle Rush and Lichess's Puzzle Storm.
set.tip.load_lichess_s_puzzle_database: Load Lichess's puzzle database so Puzzle Mode plays the KNOWN solution instead of the engine's guess. The engine's best move and the puzzle's intended move are not always the same, and only one of them scores. Lichess only -- Chess.com's Puzzle Rush positions are not in this file. The database is not bundled (it is about a gigabyte), so download it yourself and pick the file here. It is stored on this machine and nothing is ever sent anywhere.
set.tip.mephisto_takes_control_of_the: Mephisto takes control of the mouse pointer to perform automated moves. NOTE: mephisto-clicker.py (in "src/scripts") must be running for this to work. You may need to grant specific permissions for PyAutoGUI depending on your setup (do a google search for this).
set.tip.humanize_move_mix_how_often: Humanize move mix: how often each quality of move is played. Make the seven values add up to 100 -- the Total row shows what to add or remove. Each category is a band of how-much-worse-than-best, set in centipawns just below (Move-Quality Thresholds); a rolled category plays a random move inside its band, or the best move if nothing that bad exists. Nothing past the Blunder threshold is ever played, and blunders never fire in an already-decided game. Giving a share to any category worse than the near-best (Third line and below) makes the engine search a wider list so it has a move that bad to choose from -- otherwise that roll just replays the top move. That costs search depth, so a pure Top + Second mix keeps the cheaper search. Changes apply to the very next move, no reload needed.
set.tip.how_much_worse_than_the: How much worse than the best move each category may be, in centipawns (100cp = 1 pawn). Each is the top of its band; the bottom is the category above it, so Second line is 0 up to its value, Third from there up to its value, and so on. The accuracy % under each is what a move that bad scores on Lichess's own move-accuracy formula (from an equal position); the win-drop % is Lichess's move-quality measure -- ~10% = Inaccuracy, ~20% = Mistake, ~30% = Blunder. The defaults sit exactly on those boundaries.
set.tip.mephisto_will_always_wait_at: Mephisto will always wait at least this long after fully evaluating a position (determined by Search Time) to make a move.
set.tip.mephisto_will_wait_a_random: Mephisto will wait a random extra amount of time, up to this amount, on top of Simulated Think Time.
set.tip.mephisto_will_always_take_at: Mephisto will always take at least this long to perform the mouse actions of a single move.
set.tip.mephisto_will_take_a_random: Mephisto will take a random extra amount of time, up to this amount, on top of Simulated Move Time.

set.tip.language: The language of the panel and these settings. Engine names, board themes and chess notation stay as they are.
set.tip.puzzle_capture: Read the solution off the puzzle page itself. These sites hand their own client the answer -- they check your moves locally -- so it is already in the tab. Nothing is requested and nothing is sent; only what the page was already given is read. A solution is used only if it replays legally AND belongs to the position on the board, so a mismatch means the engine plays as usual. Off by default.
set.puzzle_capture_cdp: Use the debugger to catch solutions
set.tip.puzzle_capture_cdp: Read the solution reliably, by watching the page's own network traffic through Chrome's debugger. Without this, reading solutions off the page only works when the extension loads before the site does, which on some puzzle modes it never does - so the answer is a coin toss. The cost is that Chrome shows its yellow 'being debugged' bar while a puzzle page is open. Needs Read solutions from the page. Off by default.
set.note.how_often_each_quality_of: How often each quality of move is played. The seven shares must total 100. Each threshold is how much worse than best that band may be, in centipawns.
set.note.giving_a_share_to_anything: Giving a share to anything below the near-best bands makes the engine search a wider list so a move that bad exists to choose from - that costs search depth. A pure Top + Second mix keeps the cheaper search.
set.note.priority_time_mirror_clock: Priority - Time: Mirror ▸ Clock ▸ Humanize ▸ Search Time. Move: Book ▸ Humanize ▸ engine best.
panel.reload_the_page: Reload this page - the extension was updated
panel.no_site_access: No access to this site - check the extension's permissions
panel.fourpc_needs_engine: Select the Tetrarch engine to analyse 4-player chess
panel.tetrarch_setup: Tetrarch is not installed yet - see the README section "Four-player chess" for macOS, Linux and Windows setup

set.tip.chrome_never_updates_an_unpacked: Chrome never updates an extension you loaded yourself, so Mephisto can do it instead: download the small update archive from its releases page and write it straight into this extension's own folder. Turning this on asks Chrome for permission to download from that one repository - nothing is ever installed without you pressing Install.
set.note.updates_are_applied_in_place: Updates are applied in place, which is the point: your extension ID never changes, so the native engine hosts you installed keep working, and the bundled engines are left alone - the download is about 6 MB rather than 585. Choose the folder you loaded as an unpacked extension once; Chrome remembers it. After an update, reload any game tab you had open.
set.note.updates_permission_scope: The permission covers only this project's release downloads. Switching this off gives it back.
panel.update_install_now: Update available - v{latest} (you have v{current}) - click to install
set.tip.four_player_mode: Which rules the four-player board is played under. Auto-detect reads it from chess.com's own mode label, which is a guess about someone else's markup - set it yourself when that guess is wrong. It changes the rules the search runs under: promotion is the 8th rank in free-for-all and the 11th in Teams. Tetrarch searches Teams only.
set.tip.the_trace_is_normally_quiet: The trace is normally quiet while the game tab is focused, so ordinary play does not fill the console. That is the right default and the wrong thing to have to guess at: turn this on to see every decision as it happens, in the service worker's console. Costs nothing but noise.
set.note.the_panel_s_clipboard_button: The panel's clipboard button copies a report you can paste straight into a bug report: version, engine, what was detected, why the last move was or was not played, and the last 200 trace lines. It deliberately carries no addresses and nothing that identifies you - no full URL, no query string, no extension id.
set.note.every_update_is_undoable: Every update is undoable. Before anything is overwritten the new version is written to a staging folder, and the files it replaces are copied to a backup - so Roll Back puts the previous version straight back, and an update interrupted halfway can be finished without downloading it again. One generation is kept, and the bundled engines are never part of it.
panel.tip.pace_to_clock: Shrink the SIMULATED delay (the think pause and the cursor travel) when the clock gets short. Clock Mode paces the engine's search; this paces the human-looking part, which is what actually costs you time in a scramble. With clock to spare your settings are used exactly as they are: it only ever makes a move shorter, never slower, and never below the point where the click stops looking like a hand moved it.
rv.caveat: These are measurements, not a verdict. Every number below is something you can re-derive from the move table, and every one of them has an innocent explanation as well as a guilty one: short games, forced sequences, pre-moves and blitz all push the same numbers up. One game is never enough to conclude anything, and this page cannot see the things a real investigation uses. If you think someone is cheating, report them to the site and let it look.
rv.tip.pgn: Paste a PGN, or load a .pgn file. Chess.com and Lichess exports both work, including the clock comments -- those are where the time-usage numbers come from. A file holding several games gives you a list to pick from. Nothing is uploaded: the text stays in this page and the analysis runs here.
rv.tip.fetch_from: Fetch a player's recent games from the site's public API. Public data only -- the same games anyone can see on their profile -- and no login. The request goes out from this extension page, so the game site never sees it.
rv.tip.engine: Which engine judges the game. The WASM builds run inside the extension and need nothing installed. The native entries are the full-power local engines and are much faster, but only appear once their host is installed and answering -- and they take a time budget only, never a depth.
rv.tip.budget: How hard the engine works on EACH position. Depth is the better choice when you want to compare two reviews, and with Threads set to 1 it is reproducible: three depth-14 searches of the same position agreed exactly on one thread and disagreed on four, because a multi-threaded search explores in a different order every time. Time runs from 1 to 60 seconds per position, and one notch past 60 removes the clock entirely: the engine is told `go infinite` and keeps thinking about the position until you press Stop, which scores it with whatever depth it reached and ends the run. A game is roughly 2 positions per move, so 80 positions at 1s is about a minute and a half.
rv.tip.lines: How many alternatives the engine keeps per position. More lines let the review say where your move ranked rather than only whether it was the best one, and they are what the board's coloured arrows show. They also cost search: 5 lines is meaningfully slower than 1 at the same depth.
rv.tip.human_model: An optional second pass with Maia, a network trained to predict what a HUMAN of a given rating plays -- not what is best. It answers a different question from the engine: how expected was this move for a player at this level. It roughly doubles the run time.
rv.tip.opening_book: Look the opening up in the Lichess masters database, so book moves are named rather than scored. It stops at the first position the database does not know, so it is a handful of requests at the start of the game and nothing after that.
rv.tip.strength: Which rating best explains the moves that were actually played. The human model is asked at every rating it has, and the one whose predictions were least surprised is the estimate. Needs a human model selected above, and costs one pass per rating over the whole game. It is a STRENGTH estimate and NOT a fair-play measurement: a player using an engine reads as stronger, which is the opposite of an accusation.
rv.tip.human_report: A second reading of the same game by the human model instead of the engine: how EXPECTED each move was from a player of that rating, rather than how good it was. Needs a human model selected above, and costs the pass it runs. Off by default.
rv.tip.batch: Analyse EVERY game in the box rather than the one picked above, and add a summary that pools each player's numbers across all of them. One game cannot answer a fair-play question; a season of them starts to. The engine is loaded once for the whole batch, so it is much cheaper than running them one at a time.
set.tip.lichess_token: Lichess now requires a token on the opening explorer -- without one it answers 401 and both Opening Explorer and Play Book Moves stop working. Make a personal token at lichess.org/account/oauth/token/create with NO scopes ticked: the explorer only needs to know a request has an owner. It is stored on this machine like every other setting, never sent anywhere but lichess, and is left out of Copy Diagnostics and of an exported settings file.
set.tip.puzzle_move_delay: How long a DATABASE move waits before its first click. Every other move has a search in front of it, and that search is what lets the board finish animating; a known solution has none, so without a pause the click goes out while the opponent's reply is still sliding across the board and the move is dropped as a mismatch. Raise it if moves are being dropped on a slow page; lower it to solve faster. 0 disables the pause.
set.tip.puzzle_auto_next: Press Chess.com's Next Puzzle button for you when a puzzle ends, so a session runs without you. Off by default, and it also needs Puzzle Mode and Autoplay -- advancing while you are solving by hand would take the board away mid-thought. Only on the rated and learning puzzle pages: Puzzle Rush and Streak move on by themselves, and nothing else has been checked. It waits a moment first so you still see whether you got it.
set.tip.puzzle_next_delay: How long Auto-Next waits before pressing the button. The pause is there so you can see whether you solved it before the board changes -- raise it to read the position, lower it to grind. 0 presses as soon as the puzzle ends. Does nothing unless Auto-Next Puzzle is on.
panel.msg.no_eval: No evaluation - the answer was known
set.tip.drag_moves: Play moves by dragging the piece instead of clicking the two squares. Most boards accept either, so this is off by default and the two clicks stay the normal path. Chess.com's VARIANTS boards are the exception -- a quiet move works either way there, but a CAPTURE only registers as a drag -- so they always drag whatever this is set to. Turn it on if a board takes your quiet moves and silently ignores your captures. It costs the same move time either way.
set.tip.search_budget: How the search is budgeted. Time is what the clock allows. A Depth is reproducible -- the same depth is the same answer on any machine, where a millisecond budget is a different search on every one. Each keeps its own number, so switching back does not lose it.
panel.tip.search_budget: How the search is budgeted. Time is what the clock allows; a Depth is reproducible -- the same depth is the same answer on any machine. Each keeps its own number.
set.tip.move_notation: How moves are written wherever the extension shows one: the readout, the alternative lines, the arrows' labels. SAN is Nf3, UCI is g1f3 -- the same move either way.
set.tip.arrow_labels: Write each arrow's rank and its own evaluation on the board: 1 for the engine's best line, 2 upwards for the rest. Off by default -- it is useful information and it is also more ink on the board.
set.tip.arrow_opacity: How strongly the arrows are drawn, on the panel board and the page board alike. Full strength over a real board is sometimes exactly what you do not want on screen.
set.tip.board_animation: Animate the panel's own board and its overlays. Off draws every change instantly, which is steadier to read on a fast game and cheaper on a busy machine.
set.tip.live_classify: Grade the move just played and mark it on the panel board, the way a Game Review does -- Brilliant, Great, Best, Inaccuracy, Mistake, Blunder -- but live, while the game is still going. Uses the same classifier the review uses, so a verdict here is the verdict you get afterwards. Off by default: it is an opinion drawn on the board every move.
set.tip.live_classify_which: Which verdicts get a badge on the board. Turn everything off except Brilliant and Blunder to see only the moves worth a second look. This changes what is DRAWN, nothing else: the strip still counts every class, and the opponent alert has its own switch.
set.tip.live_stats: Live game grades on a strip under the eval history: a running accuracy for both sides, and each notable move named with the classifier's own verdict -- Brilliant, Miss, Blunder and the rest, worst first, in the verdict's colour. The same classifier Game Review uses, so the strip and the review afterwards agree.
panel.tip.live_stats: Live game grades on a strip under the eval history: a running accuracy for both sides, and each notable move named with the classifier's own verdict, worst first, in the verdict's colour.
set.all_releases: All releases and their notes on GitHub
panel.update_finish_setup: Update available - v{latest} - finish setting up automatic updates
set.tip.arrow_rank: Number each arrow with where its line ranks: 1 for the engine's best, 2 upwards for the rest. On by default -- with more than a couple of lines the colours alone stop being enough to tell them apart.
set.tip.forced_lines: Draw your premove-able continuation ahead of the move: while every opponent reply is their ONLY legal move, your next moves from the engine's line are drawn in blue and their forced replies in violet. The first position where the opponent has a real choice ends the chain -- everything drawn is certain given only your own choices. 0 is off.
set.tip.premove_confidence: How deep the search must agree with itself before a premove is armed: the (their move, our reply) pair must be identical at this depth, the depth before it, and the latest depth reported. 14 is the measured default. A reply that is the opponent's ONLY legal move is certified by the rules and ignores this dial entirely.
set.tip.premove_plies: How many premoves a forced sequence may queue in one click session, 1-5 (default 2). Chess.com queues them all; lichess REPLACES a queued premove rather than queueing another, so anything past the first is chess.com-only. Every queued move follows the same certainty rule as the forced-lines arrows: the opponent's replies must be their only legal move and agree with the engine's line.
set.tip.pv_walk: Draw the engine's whole line ahead on the board: every ply as a thin grey numbered arrow, so you see where the line is going, not just its first move. Grey because it is the engine's current suggestion, not a certainty -- forced continuations keep their own colours on top.
set.tip.pv_walk_limit: How many plies of the line PV Arrows draws, 1-50 (default 5). Past a dozen the board gets crowded fast; the ceiling exists for the rare deep endgame line.
set.tip.variant: Which chess variant the engine plays. Auto-detected on most sites; set it by hand when a page does not say.
set.tip.compute_time: How long the engine thinks per move, in milliseconds. More time means stronger play.
set.tip.compute_depth: How many plies deep the engine searches when the budget is Depth instead of time.
set.tip.multiple_lines: How many candidate lines to calculate and draw. Each extra line costs search time.
set.tip.computer_evaluation: Show the evaluation score, win percentages and depth in the panel.
set.tip.threat_analysis: Also calculate what the opponent is threatening, and draw it as a red arrow.
set.tip.autoplay: Play the engine's move for you automatically. Everything else automated depends on this.
set.tip.pieces: Which piece set the panel's own board draws with.
set.tip.board: Which board colours the panel's own board uses.
set.tip.coordinates: Show file letters and rank numbers on the panel's board.
set.tip.dark_mode: Dark colours for the settings pages and the panel.
set.tip.arrow_color_line4: Colour of the arrow for the fourth line.
set.tip.arrow_color_line5: Colour of the arrow for the fifth line and any beyond it.
set.tip.arrow_color_forced_ours: Colour of your own moves in a forced continuation.
set.tip.arrow_color_forced_theirs: Colour of the opponent's forced replies in a forced continuation.
set.tip.arrow_color_pv_walk: Colour of the numbered PV Arrows that draw the whole line ahead.
set.tip.arrow_color_threat: Colour of the arrow showing what the opponent threatens.
set.tip.arrow_color_book: Colour of the arrows for opening-book moves.
an.tip.time: How hard the engine works on each position. Time: it thinks that many seconds, and the last notch is no limit at all -- it keeps thinking until you move on. Depth: it searches exactly that many plies deep and stops, the same answer on any machine.
an.idle: Set up a position, or just start playing on the board.
an.tip.engine: Which engine analyses the position, for as long as the budget below allows.
an.tip.human: The human model shown beside the engine: what a player of this rating would most likely play here.
an.tip.lines: How many engine lines to list and draw on the board.
an.tip.threads: CPU threads the analysis engine may use.
an.tip.band: Which rating the human model plays at. Maia 1 has a net per band; Maia 3 is one net with a dial.
an.tip.hash: Hash memory for the analysis engine. More helps a long search on one position.
an.tip.wdl: Show the engine's win, draw and loss percentages beside the board.
an.tip.book: Show book moves for the position from a book you load below.
set.tip.grind_mode: Lichess and Chess.com, and only while Autoplay is on. When a game finishes, Mephisto clicks the button that starts the next one -- "New opponent" on Lichess, "New 1 min" (whatever your time control is) on Chess.com -- so a session keeps going without you. The delay below is your window to stop it: close the tab, navigate away or switch this off during it and no new game is searched for. If the button is not where it was expected, nothing happens and the game simply stays finished.
set.tip.grind_delay: How long to wait after a game ends before the next one is started. This is the window in which you can stop it -- 0 starts immediately, and the maximum is 600 seconds.
set.tip.threat_human: Beside the engine's best answer to your move, show what a HUMAN of the rating below would most likely reply -- Maia-3's prediction about the opponent you are actually facing, not the strongest reply on the board. Standard chess only; needs Show Threat Analysis.
set.tip.threat_human_elo: The rating the human reply is predicted at: 600-2600, any value - Maia-3 is one net with a live rating dial, so nothing is snapped.
an.tip.variant: Which rules this board plays by. Loading a PGN with a Variant tag sets it for you. Fairy-only variants switch the engine to Fairy-Stockfish; the human model and the tablebase are standard chess only.
an.tip.engine2: A second engine on the same position, beside the first. The question it answers: does the small net see what the big one sees?
panel.msg.resyncing: The engine answered for a different position - re-reading the board.
panel.msg.engine_quiet: The engine went quiet - restarting the search.
panel.fen.auto_flipped: Read from screen - Black was at the bottom, so the board was turned round. Flip board undoes it.
set.tip.vision_threads: How many CPU cores the screen reader may use. It runs a large model on every read, and while it FOLLOWS a board it does that over and over -- so this is a budget, not a speed dial: two cores read a board in about three quarters of a second, six in about six tenths. Takes effect the next time the engine host starts.
panel.msg.net_needs_lines: Safety net needs more than one line
set.tip.safety_net: For when the moves are yours. Instead of telling you the best move, it reports the SET of moves that keep the result -- and in its quiet mode it says nothing at all until that set gets small enough to be a warning. Needs Multiple Lines above 1, since the set is drawn from the lines the engine was asked for.
set.tip.safety_net_mode: Quiet: silent while the move a HUMAN of the Human Reply Rating would likely play here still holds -- it speaks only when your likely move drops the game (and, until Maia has answered, when only a few moves are left). It never nags about a position that is already lost, and a forced move is no warning. Live: always shows the moves that keep the result while it is your turn. The set is ordered by how likely a human is to play each move.
set.tip.safety_net_drop: How much of your winning chances a move may cost and still count as holding, in win% -- the same ruler the Game Review judges by, where 5 is an inaccuracy, 10 a mistake and 20 a blunder.
set.tip.safety_net_max: Quiet mode's fallback while Maia has not answered yet: how few moves must be left before it speaks. Three means: say nothing unless three or fewer moves still hold. Once Maia's read of the position is in, the trigger is your likely move leaving the set, not this count.
set.tip.arrow_color_human_reply: Colour of the arrow showing what a human of the chosen rating would most likely reply.
set.tip.arrow_color_safety_net: Colour of the arrows showing the moves that keep the result, when Playing with a Net is on.
set.tip.bot_tricks: Adds a Bot game row to the panel on chess.com's Play Computer page. A game against a bot there is decided in the browser, not on a server, so the page will accept a whole game handed to it move by move - and will accept a draw nobody offered. Off everywhere else, and the row does not exist while this is off.
set.tip.bot_trick_delay: Roughly how long between the handed-over moves, in milliseconds. Jittered by about a third either way on purpose: chess.com keeps a per-move clock time in the game archive, and eighty moves at exactly the same interval is a pattern no human produces. 0 plays the whole game at once.
set.tip.bot_trick_pgn: Paste a PGN to add your own game to the dropdown - one of your own from chess.com, or any game you like. It has to end in checkmate or a draw: a game that finished by resignation stops with the bot still to move, and it will then answer for real. The panel says so rather than half-playing it.
panel.bot.pgn_empty: Paste a game into Settings first.
panel.bot.pgn_unreadable: No moves found in that PGN.
panel.bot.no_game: No game to play - choose one first.
panel.bot.drawn: The bot accepted a draw it was never offered.
panel.bot.wrong_page: Bot tricks only work on the Play Computer page.
panel.bot.off: Turn Bot Tricks on in Settings first.
panel.bot.no_board: No bot game on this page yet - start one.
panel.bot.not_start: Only from the starting position - start a new bot game.
panel.bot.no_side: Could not tell which colour you are playing.
panel.bot.refused: The page refused it ({why}) - chess.com may have closed this.
panel.bot.wrong_colour_white: That game is a win for black, and you are playing white.
panel.bot.wrong_colour_black: That game is a win for white, and you are playing black.
set.tip.bot_trick_game: Which game to hand the bot. Every line here ends the game - a checkmate, or a draw the client claims itself - because a game that ended in resignation would stop with the bot still to move and it would then answer for real. Auto picks one that wins for whichever colour you were dealt. The panel's own dropdown sets the same thing.
panel.bot.no_library: No games loaded - reload the extension
set.tip.streamer_alert: Say so in the panel when the opponent is live-streaming the game right now. Both sites publish this themselves -- lichess says whether a player is streaming, chess.com publishes who is live -- so nothing here watches a stream. It is a NOTICE and nothing else: it changes no setting and plays no differently. Off by default because it asks the site about your opponent by name, once per game, from the extension rather than from the game tab.
panel.msg.opp_streaming: {user} is streaming this game right now
set.tip.analysis_limit: What bounds the search when there is no move to play -- Autoplay off, Help Mode, Manual Mode, or a ponder on the opponent's turn. That search has always run until the position changed; it still does, because the slider's far right is No Limit in every mode. Depth and Nodes are reproducible (the same search on any machine), Time is not. On a native engine the budget is capped at 60 seconds whatever the unit, so a nodes limit that cannot be reached in a minute ends there.
set.tip.analysis_limit_value: How much of the unit above one analysis search may spend: 1-60 plies, 1-60 seconds, or 1M-1B nodes on a logarithmic scale. The far right is No Limit -- the search deepens until the position changes, which is what it has always done.
set.tip.class_on_board: The same verdict, drawn on the SITE's board instead of the panel's -- a badge on the square the move landed on, sized to that board. Its own switch, and independent of the one above: the badge appears on the real board whether or not the panel's little board is also carrying one. The 'Show which' filter applies to both.
set.tip.playstyle: A character, not a strength - ten of them, chosen among the lines the engine already found. Attacking prefers the forcing move (check, capture, promotion), Ultra attacking goes further and throws pieces at the king, Quiet takes the calm move, Greedy the most material, Space the move that gains ground, Sacrifice the one that offers material the opponent may take, Safe the one that leaves nothing hanging, Drawish the line closest to equality, and Disrespect the rude one - a second queen, a sacrifice made while already winning, an opening on the rim, a king strolling toward theirs. Never at a cost: at most 35 centipawns, or on a human net two thirds of the top move's probability, so even Disrespect only plays moves the engine calls equal to the best. Needs Multi Lines 2 or more - with one line there is nothing to choose between. Balanced is the engine's own pick.
panel.tip.autoplay: Plays the move on the board for you. With it off the panel only analyses - everything else here is about a move that is going to be played.
panel.tip.engine: Which engine analyses. (local) needs the native host installed and is the fastest; WASM runs inside the browser; (online) sends the position to someone else's machine.
panel.tip.move_time_var: How long the move waits before it is played, and how much that wait varies at random. The search happens inside this time, not after it.
panel.tip.puzzle_mode: Plays a puzzle's whole solution instead of one move, and turns itself on when you open a puzzle page. Setting it by hand is never overridden.
panel.tip.bot_game: Hands a chess.com bot a finished game to walk into, move by move. Only from the starting position of a fresh bot game.
panel.tip.variant: Which rules the position is judged by. Only the Fairy engines play the exotic ones; the mainline Stockfishes play standard chess and Chess960.
panel.tip.fourpc_mode: Which four-player game this is. Auto-detect reads it off the page; only Teams is actually analysed.
panel.tip.threads: How many CPU threads the engine may use. More is stronger up to the cores you actually have; past that it is slower, not faster.
panel.tip.multi_lines: How many candidate lines the engine reports. More lines means each one is searched less deeply.
panel.tip.memory: The engine's hash table. Bigger helps long searches; bigger than the machine can spare hurts everything.
panel.tip.copy_diagnostics: Copy diagnostics: version, engine, what was detected, why the last move was or was not played, and the recent trace. Paste it into a bug report - it contains no addresses and nothing that identifies you.
panel.tip.turn_switch: Whose turn to move - tap to flip if it's wrong (puzzles / custom positions).
panel.tip.maia2_elos: Maia-2 plays a MATCHUP, not a level: one model that takes your rating and your opponent's, so the same position is answered differently by a 1200 facing a 2000 than by a 2000 facing a 1200. Steps of 50, and both apply instantly (no reload).
panel.tip.skill_level: Pygin's own strength dial, 0-40. It is NOT an Elo scale and not a cap: 40 is full strength and byte-identical to leaving the option alone, while a lower level caps the search depth and adds a random bias that grows with how far a move trails the best one - so a weak level picks a worse move on purpose. Applies instantly (no reload).
set.tip.skill_level: Pygin's own strength dial (sent as the UCI option `Skill Level`), 0-40. NOT an Elo scale and not a cap: 40 is full strength and is byte-identical to never sending the option, while a lower level caps the search depth and adds a random bias that grows with how far a move trails the best - so a weak level picks a worse move on purpose. Pygin refuses UCI_Elo deliberately, because no campaign has fitted that curve for it.
set.tip.tb_show: At 7 pieces or fewer the engine and the tablebase both answer, and they answer different kinds of question - one searches, the other knows. This is who gets the screen. BOTH draws the tablebase move as its own amber arrow beside the engine's numbered lines and prints both readings on the evaluation line. TABLEBASE ONLY leaves the solved move alone on the board. ENGINE ONLY keeps the arrows and the score the engine's. Display only: the tablebase move is proved and the engine's is not, so it is still the move that gets played, and the readout still names it.
set.tip.arrow_color_tb: Colour of the arrow for the endgame tablebase's move. Deliberately unlike the numbered engine lines: a solved move is a different kind of answer from a searched one.
panel.tip.engine_id: What is actually loaded right now: the engine build the panel asked for, and the neural net it reported loading. A build and a net are two different things - a dev Stockfish with an old net is not the engine you think you are running, and nothing else on this panel would tell you.
panel.tip.copy_analysis: Copy the position and what the engine says about it as plain text: the FEN, the score and depth, and every candidate line with its own score. For a note, a message or an issue - it is the panel's answer in a form you can paste.
panel.tip.reanalyse: Throw away the current answer and search this same position again from scratch. For when a setting changed under a search, or the readout looks stale and you would rather not move a piece to find out. The board is not touched.
panel.tip.opacity: How solid the panel itself is drawn, 40-100%. Below 100 the board underneath shows through, which is the point: the panel can sit over the game instead of beside it. Remembered per site, along with where you dragged it.
panel.tip.dock: Park the panel against an edge of the window and keep it there while you play - it follows a resize instead of ending up half off screen. Free leaves it exactly where you drag it, which is what it has always done. Remembered per site.
set.tip.refute: After a move of YOURS that grades an inaccuracy or worse, draw the line that punishes it - the opponent's whole best continuation, ply by ply, in its own dark red. The badge tells you a move was bad; this shows what it loses. It reads the same graded history Move Classification uses, so switching it on switches that recording on too.
set.tip.contempt: For a game you have to WIN. The engine is perfectly happy with a draw, and the repetition it offers at 0.00 is half a point gone. With this on, a move that ENDS THE GAME as a draw on the spot - a threefold, a fifty-move, a stalemate, insufficient material - is passed over for the best move that does not, as long as that move costs no more than the Contempt setting below. When the top move is not one of those, nothing changes: this never touches an ordinary position. NEEDS MULTI LINES 2 OR MORE, and it never walks into a mate to dodge a draw.
set.tip.contempt_cp: How many centipawns avoiding the draw is worth, 0 to 200. 30 is a third of a pawn: enough to take a real game over a repetition, not enough to spoil the position to do it.
set.tip.refute_plies: How many plies of the punishing line to draw, 1 to 6.
set.tip.second_opinion: Ask a human-trained net what a player of the Human Reply Rating would play HERE, beside the engine's own answer, and say so when the two come apart - when the engine's move is one this rating almost never finds. Two questions, not one: what is best, and what a person actually plays. Costs one forward pass on a net the threat reply already loads, so with Human Reply on it is free. Standard chess only.
set.tip.opp_prep: What THIS opponent has played in the position in front of you, from their own recent public games on the site you are on. People repeat their repertoire, and a line they have played eleven times is one they will play again. LONGER GAMES ONLY - it needs a clock reading of five minutes or more, because it costs a fetch and is only worth having while you still have time to use it. The request is made by the extension's worker, so your game tab never carries a lookup about the person you are playing.
set.tip.player_book: Build an opening book from a real person's public games and PLAY it, weighted by how often they played each move. Put your own username in the box for your own repertoire, or anyone else's - a titled player, a streamer - to borrow theirs. Works on lichess and chess.com; a bare name means the site you are on, and you can spell it out as lichess:name or chesscom:name. It is prep, not statistics: no engine veto, and it simply runs out past the opening, where the engine's move stands again. The lookup is made by the extension's worker, once per player per session.
set.tip.player_book_user: Whose games to build the book from. A bare username means the site you are playing on; write lichess:name or chesscom:name to say which archive to ask.
set.tip.player_book_wins: Build the book only from the games that player WON. On by default, and it is what makes your own games usable: a book from every game you ever played contains every opening you lost with. Turn it off to take the whole repertoire, wins and losses alike - worth it for a strong player whose games are all worth having.
set.tip.game_log: Write the panel's own evaluation of every ply into Copy PGN, in the comment format both sites already read: {[%eval 0.31] [%depth 22]}. It is what the panel measured DURING the game at whatever depth it reached, not a re-analysis - Game Review is for that. Only plies that were really evaluated get a comment.
set.tip.mirror_ratio: What share of the opponent's own think Mirror Time spends, 50-150%. It was fixed at 90, which pulls a little ahead on the clock every move but still lets a slow opponent set your pace. Above 100 deliberately spends MORE than they do, which is worth it in a long game where the extra think buys more than the seconds cost. Whatever you set, being BEHIND on the clock still cuts the target by 30%, so a high ratio cannot dig the hole deeper. Only used while Mirror Time is on.
set.tip.time_trouble: One switch for a scramble: below the threshold the search is capped at a quarter of a second and the simulated human delay collapses to the floor a click still needs. What loses games at ten seconds is the cursor travel and the think pause, not the depth. Works whether or not Clock Mode or Mirror Time is on, and it overrides both - they are budgeting a clock this says is nearly gone.
set.tip.complexity_clock: Think by how hard the position is. A fixed think time spends the same seconds on a position with one move as on one with five; a person bangs out the obvious move and sits on the hard one. This reads how far apart the engine's own top two lines are - free, because the search already produced it - and stretches the think up to 1.6x when they are within 15cp of each other, or cuts it to 0.6x when one move is ahead by more than 250cp. It scales whatever else is deciding the think, Humanize included, and the clock caps still sit above it. NEEDS MULTI LINES 2 OR MORE, and it never stretches a reflex.
set.tip.auto_resign: Resign when the game is gone. The score has to stay below the threshold for three of YOUR turns running, so one deep line at one depth cannot end a game. Needs Autoplay, presses the site's own resign button and confirms it, and does it once - after that no move is played into a game you have resigned. Off unless you switch it on, for the obvious reason.
set.tip.auto_resign_cp: How far behind counts as gone, in centipawns, 100 to 3000. 900 is a queen.
set.tip.auto_draw: Offer a draw in a position neither side can change: the score within the threshold below, for three of YOUR turns running, and past move 20 - nobody offers a draw on move six. Needs Autoplay, and it offers ONCE per game, because a declined offer repeated every move is what gets people muted. The move is still played: offering a draw is something you do alongside a move, not instead of one.
set.tip.session_stats: What this browser session has actually done: games finished, moves played, the average time each one really waited, and your accuracy across the finished games. It is the number the sliders cannot answer themselves - a 2.4s average against a 3-second think time tells you what the pacing modes are really doing. It lives as long as the panel does: a reload starts a new session, and nothing is stored.
set.tip.auto_draw_cp: How level counts as level, in centipawns either way, 0 to 100. 20 is a fifth of a pawn.
set.tip.human_times: Draw the think delay from the shape real move times have instead of from a flat band. The Think Time and Variance sliders draw evenly between two edges and stop dead at both; a person's move times pile up just under a short typical value and trail away to the right, with a few moves taking several times the median. This keeps the AVERAGE your sliders describe and changes only the shape, so a histogram of your move times looks like a person's. Works with Humanize on (it reshapes its think) and off. The cursor travel is left alone - a hand does not move that way.
set.tip.time_trouble_at: The clock reading, in seconds, below which Time Trouble Mode takes over. 5 to 120.
set.tip.pv_keys: Walk the engine's line with the LEFT and RIGHT arrow keys on the panel's own board. Right plays the engine's best move for the position you are looking at and searches on from there, so holding it walks the whole variation; left steps back. OFF by default, and while it is off the arrow keys are left entirely alone - both chess sites use them for their own move navigation, and a key the panel does not act on is never swallowed. Rebindable like every other hotkey.
set.tip.arrow_colorblind: Replace every arrow colour above with the Okabe-Ito palette, an eight-hue set chosen to stay distinguishable under the common forms of colour blindness. The shipped defaults separate lines by red against green, which is the one pair that collapses. Restore Defaults on this page puts the original colours back.
panel.msg.second_opinion_off: A {elo} plays {move} ({pct}%) - and almost never the engine's
set.tip.arrow_color_refute: Colour of the line that punishes one of your own mistakes. Its own dark red: it is the only thing on the board that describes something that already happened, rather than something to play.
